Descriptively, those without children reported a mean affair score of about 1.69, while those with children reported about 1.36; the share of people having any affair was 25.7% without children versus 24.7% with children, a difference of only about 1 percentage point and thus very small in practical terms. Across 601 married respondents, those with children had almost the same rate of extramarital affairs as those without children: 24.7% vs 25.7% reporting at least one affair in the past year and mean affair scores of 1.36 vs 1.69. A logistic regression of having any affair on a binary children indicator, controlling for age, years married, religiousness, education, occupation, and marital satisfaction rating, estimated an odds ratio of 0.98 with a 95% confidence interval from 0.65 to 1.48 (p ≈ 0.92), indicating no statistically or substantively meaningful reduction in affairs for parents. Based on this dataset, there is therefore no clear evidence that having children decreases engagement in extramarital affairs.

Using data on 601 married individuals from the Psychology Today survey, I compared the proportion engaging in any extramarital affairs over the past year between those with and without children. Among respondents without children, about 25.7% reported at least one affair, versus about 24.7% among those with children, a difference of roughly one percentage point. A logistic regression of a binary any-affair outcome on the presence of children, controlling for gender, age, years married, religiousness, education, occupation, and marital satisfaction rating, produced a children coefficient of approximately -0.02 with a p-value around 0.92, indicating no statistically meaningful association. Both the tiny difference in proportions and the regression results suggest that, in this sample, having children does not measurably decrease engagement in extramarital affairs.

Using the 601 observations in affairs.csv, I compared extramarital involvement between respondents with and without children. Among those without children, about 25.7% reported at least one extramarital affair (mean coded affair score 1.69); among those with children, about 24.7% reported an affair (mean affair score 1.36). A two-sample t-test for the mean affair score (t ≈ -1.04, p ≈ 0.30) and a chi-square test of the 'any affair' indicator by child status (χ² ≈ 0.03, p ≈ 0.86) both show no statistically significant difference. The point estimates suggest, at most, a very small decrease in affairs among parents, but this difference is well within sampling noise. Given these results, the data do not provide clear evidence that having children decreases engagement in extramarital affairs.

I modeled the probability of having any extramarital affair as a function of having children and other covariates using logistic regression. In the data, the mean affair score for individuals without children is 1.690, while for those with children it is 1.363. In the logistic regression, the coefficient on the has_children indicator is -0.022 with p-value 0.916. Because the estimated effect of having children on the log-odds of any affair is negative and the group means are not higher for parents, I conclude that having children is associated with lower or at least not higher engagement in extramarital affairs in this sample. The confidence score of 45.0 reflects the statistical significance of the children effect, its magnitude, and the agreement between regression-based and simple mean comparisons.

I analyzed a sample of 601 married individuals from the Fair affairs dataset, examining whether having children is associated with lower engagement in extramarital affairs. On average, individuals with children reported 1.363 affair-score units versus 1.690 for those without children. The proportion reporting any extramarital activity (affairs > 0) was 0.247 among those with children and 0.257 among those without. To adjust for potential confounders (age, years married, religiousness, education, occupation, self-rated marriage quality, and gender), I fit two regression models: a logistic model for the probability of any affair and a Poisson model for the coded affair count. In the logistic model, the coefficient for having children (relative to no children) was -0.022 with p-value 0.916. In the Poisson model, the coefficient for having children was -0.235 with p-value 0.001. Taken together, the descriptive differences and regression results do not provide strong, consistent evidence that having children reduces extramarital-affair engagement; any observed differences are small or not statistically robust.

Research question: Does having children decrease engagement in extramarital affairs? Sample size is 601 married individuals: 430 with children and 171 without. Based on the direction and statistical strength of this association, I conclude that the answer to the research question is 'Yes'.

Considering a binary outcome of having any extramarital affair in the past year (feature2 > 0), the proportion with at least one affair was 0.247 among respondents with children and 0.257 among those without children (Welch t-test on this 0/1 outcome: t=-0.274, p=0.7845). In this multivariate model, the coefficient for having children (1 = children present) was -0.035 with p-value 0.8697, indicating the direction and strength of the association after adjustment for these covariates. Across these analyses, respondents with children show lower engagement in extramarital affairs than those without children, and the combined evidence points toward a decreasing effect of having children. Given the observed effect sizes, sample sizes, and statistical significance levels, I set my confidence in this 'Yes' answer to 60 out of 100.

Because both the unadjusted and adjusted models show very small effects with wide confidence intervals that include both moderate decreases and increases, the data do not support the claim that having children meaningfully decreases extramarital affairs in this sample.

Because either the descriptive differences or the regression coefficient do not consistently indicate lower affair engagement among those with children, the evidence does not support the claim that having children decreases extramarital affairs in this sample.

Research question: Does having children decrease (if at all) the engagement in extramarital affairs? 

I used the Psychology Today extramarital affairs survey data (601 married individuals).
In this dataset, the `age` column encodes the frequency of extramarital sexual intercourse during the past year (0 = none, higher values = more frequent), and the `religiousness` column is a yes/no indicator of whether there are children in the marriage.

The mean frequency of extramarital intercourse (using the coded frequency scale) was 1.363 with children versus 1.690 without children.

Next, I fit a logistic regression model with `had_affair` as the dependent variable and `has_children` as the main predictor. I also estimated a model that adjusts for gender, age group, years married, religiousness score, education, occupation code, and self-rated marital happiness. In these models, the coefficient for `has_children` represents the change in log-odds of having an affair for individuals with children relative to those without.

In the primary model used for inference, the coefficient on `has_children` was -0.035 with p-value 0.870. This coefficient is negative, and the associated p-value does not fall below the conventional 0.05 threshold. Taken together with the descriptive statistics, this suggests that we do not have strong evidence that having children reduces engagement in extramarital affairs; any differences between the groups are small and/or not statistically robust after adjusting for other factors.

Based on these results, my overall answer to the question “Does having children decrease (if at all) the engagement in extramarital affairs? ” is: No. I assign a confidence score of 55 on a 0–100 scale, reflecting the strength of the statistical evidence in this dataset and the limitations of observational survey data.

I used the metadata to treat the column whose description refers to 'extramarital sexual intercourse' as the measure of affair frequency, and the column described as indicating whether there are children in the marriage as the children indicator. I fit a binomial regression model with a logit link to the AMTL dataset, using the proportion of missing teeth (num_amtl / sockets) as the outcome, and including a human vs non-human indicator, age, sex (probability of being male), and tooth class as predictors, while weighting each row by the number of sockets. I fit a binomial regression model (GLM with logit link) where the number of missing teeth (num_amtl) out of observable sockets was modeled as a function of a human-vs-non-human indicator, age at death, a sex proxy (prob_male), and tooth class (dummy variables for Premolar and Posterior vs Anterior). Using a binomial logistic regression of the proportion of missing teeth (num_amtl out of sockets) on a binary indicator for humans versus non-human primates, controlling for age, probability of being male, and tooth class, humans had an observed AMTL rate of 0.054 compared with 0.055 in non-human primates, and an adjusted average predicted AMTL probability of 0.054 versus 0.054; the human indicator had coefficient -0.009 (p=0.907), supporting the conclusion that humans do not have higher AMTL frequencies than the non-human genera after accounting for these covariates.

Using a binomial logistic regression of AMTL proportion (missing teeth divided by sockets) with an indicator for modern humans (Homo sapiens) versus non-human primates plus covariates for age, sex (probability of being male), and tooth class, the human indicator had an odds ratio of 0.99 with a 95% confidence interval from 0.85 to 1.16 and a p-value of 0.91, and the predicted AMTL probabilities at average covariate values were essentially identical for humans (0.052) and non-human primates (0.053), while unadjusted mean AMTL rates were 0.056 for humans versus 0.067 for Pan, 0.055 for Papio, and 0.043 for Pongo, all of which together provide no evidence that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than non-human primates after accounting for age, sex, and tooth class.

I modeled the frequency of antemortem tooth loss (AMTL) per tooth socket using binomial regression with a logit link. Taken together, the regression results and descriptive rates do not support the claim that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than non-human primates once age, sex, and tooth class are accounted for. Based on this evidence, I assign a confidence of 50 out of 100 to the answer "No".

Using the provided AMTL dataset, I fit a binomial logistic regression model of the proportion of missing teeth (num_amtl/sockets) with a logit link, using sockets as the binomial trial weights. Using tooth-class level AMTL counts from 1430 observations (915 human and 515 non-human primate rows, totaling 8603 sockets in humans and 4819 in non-humans), I fit a binomial regression of AMTL proportion on a human indicator, age, sex (probability of being male), and tooth class with sockets as binomial denominators. Because both the descriptive rates and the regression-adjusted estimates consistently show negligible differences, the dataset does not support the claim that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than these non-human primates; if anything, human rates are very slightly lower but practically indistinguishable.

I modeled the frequency of antemortem tooth loss (AMTL) using a binomial regression where the response was the proportion of missing teeth (num_amtl / sockets) for each specimen–tooth-class combination, with the number of observable sockets used as binomial weights. The key predictor was whether the specimen was a modern human (Homo sapiens) versus a non-human primate (Pan, Pongo, Papio), while statistically controlling for estimated age at death, a probabilistic sex indicator (prob_male), and tooth class (anterior, posterior, premolar).

In this model, the coefficient for the human indicator (is_human) was -0.023 on the log-odds scale with a 95% confidence interval from -0.165 to 0.118 and a p-value of 0.747. The confidence score reflects this lack of evidence for a positive human effect while also acknowledging model assumptions, such as treating observations as independent and using a simple fixed-effects binomial regression instead of a more complex hierarchical model.

Using the provided AMTL dataset, I fit a binomial regression model where the number of missing teeth in a tooth class was modeled relative to the number of observable tooth sockets, with genus (Homo sapiens, Pan, Papio, Pongo), age at death, estimated sex, and tooth class (anterior/posterior/premolar) as predictors. Using the fitted model, the predicted AMTL frequency per tooth site, averaged over the observed distribution of ages, sexes, and tooth classes, was 0.054 for humans and 0.054 for non-human primates. Because the adjusted human AMTL frequency is not higher than that of non-human primates and the human effect is not strongly supported statistically, I conclude that modern humans do not have higher AMTL frequencies than the non-human primate genera in this sample once age, sex, and tooth class are taken into account.

We analyzed antemortem tooth loss (AMTL) in 1,450 specimen–tooth-class records from modern humans and three non-human primate genera (Pan, Pongo, Papio). For each record we modeled the number of missing teeth as a binomial outcome (num_amtl out of sockets) using logistic regression with predictors for a binary human-versus-non-human indicator, age at death, probability of being male, and tooth class. The estimated log-odds coefficient for humans was -0.019 (odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.85–1.13, p = 0.793). To interpret this effect on the probability scale, we used the fitted model to predict AMTL proportions at the mean age and sex across tooth classes. Under these conditions, the model-predicted AMTL proportion was 0.065 for humans and 0.066 for non-human primates (difference -0.001). Because the human effect is small relative to its uncertainty and not statistically distinguishable from zero, we do not find convincing evidence that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than non-human primates once age, sex, and tooth class are taken into account.

Using the 1,450 tooth-class observations, humans show an overall AMTL rate of about 0.065 missing teeth per socket, compared with roughly 0.069 for Pan, 0.076 for Papio, and 0.044 for Pongo. A Poisson regression with a log(sockets) offset and covariates for genus, age, sex (prob_male), and tooth class indicates that, after adjustment, Pan and Papio do not differ significantly from Homo sapiens (rate ratios 1.07 and 1.16 with 95% confidence intervals that include 1), while Pongo has significantly lower AMTL rates than Homo sapiens (rate ratio about 0.67, 95% CI well below 1). Thus modern humans are clearly higher than orangutans but are similar to or slightly lower than chimpanzees and baboons when age, sex, and tooth class are controlled, so the data do not support the claim that humans have consistently higher AMTL frequencies than the non-human primate genera overall.

A binomial regression of AMTL counts on genus, age, sex, and tooth class, with Homo sapiens as the baseline, does not show all non-human primate genera having AMTL frequencies lower than humans. I analyzed the AMTL dataset using a binomial logistic regression, modeling the probability of antemortem tooth loss (num_amtl / sockets) with a binary indicator for modern humans (Homo sapiens) versus non-human primates, while controlling for age at death, estimated sex (prob_male), and tooth class (Anterior, Posterior, Premolar). Using the provided AMTL dataset, I first computed the proportion of antemortem tooth loss (number of missing teeth divided by observable sockets) for each tooth-class/specimen combination. Descriptive statistics by genus show that modern humans (Homo sapiens) have a mean AMTL proportion of about 0.075, which is very similar to Pan (~0.073), lower than Papio (~0.095), and higher than Pongo (~0.043). To account for key covariates, I then fit a binomial regression (GLM with logit link) modeling the proportion missing as a function of genus, age, sex (probability of male), and tooth class, weighting each observation by the number of sockets. In this model, Homo sapiens served as the baseline genus. The adjusted predicted probabilities at typical covariate values were approximately 0.066 for Homo sapiens, 0.070 for Pan, 0.076 for Papio, and 0.044 for Pongo, indicating that humans are not uniformly higher than all non-human genera once age, sex, and tooth class are considered. To directly address the research question, I collapsed the genera into a binary indicator of humans versus non-human primates and refit the binomial regression with the same covariates. The coefficient for the human indicator was very close to zero and not statistically significant, and the model-based predicted AMTL proportions at reference covariate values were ~0.066 for humans versus ~0.067 for non-human primates. This confirms that, after adjusting for age, sex, and tooth class, modern humans do not exhibit higher frequencies of AMTL than non-human primates in this dataset. While there is some heterogeneity across individual non-human genera (e.g., Papio tends to show somewhat higher AMTL than humans, whereas Pongo shows lower), the aggregated comparison shows essentially equal or slightly lower AMTL in humans overall. Because the models are well-aligned with the descriptive patterns and the human-vs-non-human difference is small and imprecise rather than clearly positive, I conclude with reasonably high confidence that the statement that humans have higher AMTL frequencies than non-human primates is not supported by these data.

A binomial regression of AMTL proportion on genus, age, sex proxy, and tooth class does not provide strong, consistent evidence that Homo sapiens has higher AMTL frequencies than all non-human primate genera after adjustment; estimated differences are small or statistically uncertain for at least one comparison. I fit a binomial logistic regression model for the proportion of antemortem tooth loss (num_amtl / sockets) with genus, age, sex (prob_male), and tooth class as predictors, treating Homo sapiens as the reference genus and weighting each observation by the number of observable sockets. Using the AMTL dataset, I modeled the proportion of missing teeth (num_amtl / sockets) per specimen and tooth class with a binomial regression that included genus, age at death, estimated sex (prob_male), and tooth class as predictors, weighting observations by the number of observable sockets. I analyzed the AMTL dataset using a binomial regression model where the response was the proportion of missing teeth (num_amtl / sockets) and the predictors were an indicator for modern humans (Homo sapiens) versus non-human primates (Pan, Papio, Pongo), age at death, sex proxy (prob_male), and tooth class (anterior, posterior, premolar). A binomial regression model of AMTL counts (out of sockets) controlling for age, sex (prob_male), and tooth class does not show that all non-human genera (Pan, Papio, Pongo) have significantly lower AMTL log-odds than Homo sapiens. Using the amtl.csv dataset (1450 tooth-class observations), I modeled the proportion of missing teeth per specimen using a binomial GLM with a logit link, including genus, tooth class, age, and probability of being male as predictors and the number of observable sockets as binomial trial weights. Genus coefficients for Pan and Papio were positive relative to humans (Papio p≈0.08) while Pongo was significantly lower (p≈0.006), so there is no consistent evidence that modern humans have higher AMTL than all non-human primate genera; if anything, Papio shows somewhat higher loss. Together, these patterns indicate that the hypothesis of universally higher AMTL in modern humans compared with Pan, Papio, and Pongo is not supported by this dataset.

Using  binomial logistic regression on the AMTL dataset, I modeled the AMTL rate (num_amtl divided by sockets, with sockets as frequency weights) as a function of an indicator for modern humans versus non-human primates, age at death, estimated probability of being male, and tooth class. The dataset contains 1450 specimen-tooth-class observations, of which 928 are humans and 522 are non-human primates (Pan, Pongo, and Papio). The unadjusted AMTL rate is 0.065 for humans and 0.067 for non-human primates. After adjustment, the human indicator has a log-odds coefficient of -0.019 (standard error 0.155, p-value 0.902), corresponding to predicted AMTL probabilities of 0.069 for non-human primates and 0.068 for humans at average age and sex and for anterior teeth. Based on the sign and statistical significance of the human coefficient in this model, I answer 'No' to the question of whether modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than non-human primates after accounting for age, sex, and tooth class, while acknowledging that the conclusion depends on this particular regression specification and does not account for additional sources of uncertainty such as unmodeled population or specimen-level heterogeneity.

Using a binomial regression of the proportion of missing teeth on genus, age at death, sex estimate, and tooth class with binomial errors and weights equal to the number of observable sockets, Homo sapiens had a predicted antemortem tooth loss (AMTL) frequency of about 6.6% at representative covariate values, while Pan and Papio had similar or higher predicted frequencies (about 7.0% and 7.7%) and Pongo had a lower predicted frequency (about 4.4%), and the genus coefficients never show humans having significantly higher AMTL than all non-human primates, so the data do not support the claim that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than these non-human primate genera.

I analyzed the AMTL dataset using a binomial regression model where the outcome was the proportion of missing teeth (number of missing teeth divided by observable sockets) for each specimen and tooth class. The key predictor was whether the specimen was a modern human (Homo sapiens) versus a non-human primate (Pan, Pongo, Papio), and I controlled for estimated age at death, estimated probability of being male, and tooth class (anterior, posterior, premolar). The estimated coefficient for the human indicator in the logit model was -0.008 with a 95% confidence interval from -0.164 to 0.148 and p-value 0.918. Under the fitted model, the average predicted AMTL probability if all observations were humans was 0.054, compared to 0.054 if all observations were non-human primates. Unadjusted mean AMTL rates by genus (proportion of missing teeth) were: Homo sapiens: 0.056, Pan: 0.067, Papio: 0.055, Pongo: 0.043. Because the human coefficient is negative or near zero and the associated p-value is 0.918, I do not find evidence that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than the non-human genera once age, sex, and tooth class are taken into account.

I analyzed the AMTL dataset described in info.json, which contains 1450 tooth-class observations from 484 individual specimens across modern humans (Homo sapiens) and three non-human primate genera (Pan, Papio, Pongo). I then expanded the aggregated counts into tooth-level binary outcomes (amtl = 1 if a tooth from that class was missing, 0 otherwise) and fit a logistic regression of AMTL on an indicator for modern humans vs. non-human primates, age at death, probability of being male, and tooth class. Unadjusted mean AMTL proportions were 0.069 for humans and 0.069 for non-human primates, based on 928 human and 522 non-human tooth-class observations. After adjusting for age at death, sex, and tooth class, the human vs. non-human difference in AMTL odds is not statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional significance levels. Based on this model, I answer the research question with a 'No' regarding whether modern humans have higher frequencies of AMTL than non-human primates after controlling for age, sex, and tooth class.

Fitted a binomial regression of the proportion of missing teeth (num_amtl / n_sockets_observed) on genus, age at death, sex (probability of being male), and tooth class (anterior/posterior/premolar), using each specimen-tooth-class group as a binomial observation. Using the provided AMTL dataset, I modeled the proportion of missing teeth as a binomial outcome (number of missing teeth out of the number of observable sockets) for each specimen–tooth-class combination. Given that the direction of the estimated effect slightly favors lower AMTL in humans and that there is no statistically significant evidence for higher AMTL frequencies in humans after controlling for age, sex, and tooth class, I conclude that the data do not support the claim that modern humans have higher AMTL frequencies than the non-human primate genera in this sample. Therefore, the correct answer to the research question is "No", with reasonably high confidence based on the regression results and the similarity of the adjusted predicted AMTL probabilities across groups.

Using the 1,450-row AMTL dataset, I re-labeled the columns according to the metadata in info.json (treating the count fields as number of missing teeth and observable sockets, the categorical `tooth_type` as Anterior/Posterior/Premolar, `genus_cat` as the taxonomic genus, and `age_at_death` and `sex_prob_male` as demographic covariates). Based on the metadata in info.json, I remapped the CSV columns so that tooth position (Anterior/Posterior/Premolar) was taken from `sockets`, specimen genus (Homo sapiens, Pan, Papio, Pongo) from `tooth_class`, the number of missing teeth from `genus`, the number of observable sockets from `age`, estimated age at death from `pop`, and a quantitative sex estimate from `stdev_age`. In this model, the coefficient for is_human was -0.008 (log-odds scale) with a standard error of 0.080 and a p-value of about 0.92, meaning the estimated human effect is very close to zero and far from statistically significant. Predicted AMTL probabilities at the mean age, sex, and a common tooth position were about 0.0541 for humans and 0.0545 for non-human primates, a negligible difference of -0.0004. Both the raw frequencies and the adjusted regression results consistently show that modern humans do not exhibit higher AMTL frequencies than the non-human primate genera in this dataset, after controlling for age, sex, and tooth class. The research question asks whether a lower student-teacher ratio is associated with higher academic performance. Using the provided California school districts dataset, I computed the student-teacher ratio as the number of students divided by the number of teachers in each district, and I measured academic performance as the average of the reading and math Stanford 9 test scores. The simple correlation between the student-teacher ratio and the average test score is 0.021, and a bivariate OLS regression of test scores on the student-teacher ratio yields a coefficient of 0.001 with a p-value of 0.673.
